EXTRA CLASS · THE TODDLER ROOM

Welcome to the Toddler Room.

The room a one- to three-year-old already lives in, card by card: play time, mealtimes, the sleep corner, the care routines, getting dressed and the furniture that holds it together — every step-by-step lesson right here, and every card has a download button and an age pill.

HOW THIS ROOM WORKS

Thirty-five words, one room, no schedule.

The Toddler Room is a bonus class, kept deliberately beside the main learning path: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this room is here whenever a one- to three-year-old wants more. Every card names something the child already touches every day — the ball, the crib, the sippy cup, the teddy — and every step-by-step lesson right here: the word, the routine it lives in, the parent script and one small game.

The room is laid out the way toddlers live: play time first, then mealtimes, the sleep corner, the care routines, getting dressed, and the furniture that holds it all together. Every card carries an age pill — Ages 1+ for first words, Ages 2–3 for routines and pretend play — so you can start where your child is today and let the set grow with them. Dip in any order, in any mood, for two minutes at a time. Skipping this room leaves nobody behind; that is what a bonus is for.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "ball" the way toddlers learn best: the word, the object, the game — in that order, with the rolling done by both of you.

What is this?

A ball is a round toy that rolls. It is usually the first play object a toddler can name, because it moves, it responds and it never gets old.

What does it mean?

The ball lesson is really two lessons: the word "ball" attaches to a loved object, and the rolling game plants turn-taking — I roll, you roll — long before sharing is taught.

What does the child need to know?

You need the ball, a stretch of floor and three lines: the word before the action ("ball!"), the action after the word (roll), and the pause after your turn — waiting is where the toddler’s turn is born.

Why this matters

Ball is a high-frequency, low-frustration word: the object is exciting, the game is instant and a failed roll just rolls again. Words with happy loops get learned and kept.

What it teaches

First-word vocabulary, visual tracking (the eyes follow the roll), reaching and grasping, and the earliest back-and-forth rhythm that conversation will borrow.

Words to learn

ballrollchasecatchmy turnyour turn

Say this to your child

“"Ball! This is the ball. Watch — the ball rolls! Roll, roll, roll… chase it! And now: roll the ball to me. And I roll it back — my turn, your turn. Ball is the best game."”

Step by step

  1. Hold the ball still at the toddler’s eye level and say "ball" — twice, slowly. Let a hand land on it.
  2. Roll it one slow stride away. Say "roll!" as it goes — word and motion glued together.
  3. Let the chase happen. The toddler fetches; you celebrate with the word: "you found the ball!"
  4. Open your hands and ask: "roll to me?" Wait. The wait is the lesson — a returned roll is a conversation.
  5. Finish on a win, not a fade: two more rolls, then "ball sleeps now" as you park it on the shelf.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "ball" sits under a beach ball in four bright colors — red, yellow, green, blue — a picture as round and simple as the toy itself.

Ask your child

"Where is the ball?" "Can you roll the ball?" "Whose turn is it — my turn or your turn?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "baaa!", roll it back on request, or push it, sit on it and laugh — all three are the lesson working.

Out in the real world

Balls turn up everywhere: the market pile, a neighbour’s yard, the phone screen when a match is on. Name each one — "ball!" — and the word picks up fans all over town.

Try it together

Roll-and-Freeze: roll three times with turns, then call "freeze!" — both hands stop the ball. Freeze makes the stopping a game, and a child who can stop a game can start one tomorrow.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (ball) "Show me roll." (a push) "Now MY turn or YOUR turn?" A point, a push and a giggle — three ticks, lesson done.

This lesson pairs with the Ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Blanket — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "blanket" away from bedtime first — the word gets its own happy game, so when it appears at the crib rail it is already a friend.

What is this?

A blanket is the soft cover that goes over the body for sleeping — folded by day, spread over the crib by night, and known to every toddler as the cozy part of bedtime.

What does it mean?

Blanket is a routine word: it does not describe a thing so much as predict an event. Routine words are the toddler’s schedule made speakable.

What does the child need to know?

You need the blanket, a willing teddy and one rule — the game happens when nobody is tired. A word practised in daylight works at night; a word introduced at bedtime works a week later.

Why this matters

Bedtime friction is usually surprise friction. The word "blanket" said at the same moment nightly turns the cover into a countdown the toddler’s body believes.

What it teaches

Routine vocabulary, object permanence (things go under and come back), gentle-hand practice, and the self-soothing habit of a cover that means rest.

Words to learn

blanketsoftcozytucked innight-nightsleep

Say this to your child

“"Blanket! The soft, cozy blanket. Look — teddy is cold! Tuck him in… night-night, teddy. Shhh, he is sleeping. And… good morning, teddy! Again! You tuck him in this time."”

Step by step

  1. Bring the blanket to the play floor: "blanket! Soft and cozy."
  2. Tuck the teddy in: "night-night, teddy" — cover him fully, wait two seconds.
  3. Lift the blanket: "good MORNING, teddy!" The reveal is the joke; do it five times.
  4. Offer the turn: the toddler covers the teddy. Sloppy tucks are perfect tucks.
  5. At bedtime tonight, hold the same blanket and use the same words — "blanket, cozy, night-night" — so the game and the crib speak one language.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "blanket" sits under a folded blue blanket — folded the way it waits on the crib all day before it works at night.

Ask your child

"Where does the blanket go?" (on the bed / over teddy) "Who is sleeping under the blanket?" "Is the blanket soft or hard?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "nigh-nigh" while tucking, pat the blanket gently, or fetch it at bedtime unprompted — the routine word landing where it lives.

Out in the real world

Blankets live on sofas, in prams, in grandma’s house. Each sighting is a free repetition: "blanket! Cozy one." The word travels; the routine follows.

Try it together

Teddy Tuck-In: three tucks, three wake-ups, then swap roles — the toddler tucks, YOU say night-night. Reversing the roles doubles the giggles and the practice.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the blanket go?" (on the bed) "Show me soft." (a gentle pat) "Who sleeps under it?" A pat, a point, a name — the sleepy word is won.

This lesson pairs with the Blanket flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Bookshelf — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "bookshelf" as a place with a job: books sleep here, stories start here, and the walk home to the shelf is part of reading.

What is this?

A bookshelf is the shelf where books live between readings — in this room, a low shelf the toddler can reach, so choosing and returning are both the child’s own work.

What does it mean?

The bookshelf teaches belonging: books have a home, stories have a start line, and the child who puts a book back owns the whole reading loop.

What does the child need to know?

You need a reachable shelf, two or three books and the two-line ritual: "pick a book" (start) and "book goes home" (finish). The parent’s job is to point, name and wait.

Why this matters

A named shelf turns tidy-up from instruction into identity — "we are the family whose books go home." That identity survives every room the child will ever read in.

What it teaches

Choice-making (a real executive-function seed), carrying carefully, matching object to place, and the finish-a-task habit that tidying quietly builds.

Words to learn

bookshelfbookpickput backhomestory

Say this to your child

“"Bookshelf! This is where the books live. Pick a book… that one! Good choice. Let’s read… and finished! Now the book goes home — on the bookshelf. Night-night, book."”

Step by step

  1. Stand at the shelf together: "bookshelf! The books live here."
  2. Invite the choice: "pick a book — any book." Wait through the deliberation; choosing is thinking.
  3. Read anywhere — floor, lap, cushion. The shelf only bookends the story.
  4. The return march: "story finished — book goes home on the bookshelf!" Walk it back together, spine first.
  5. Close the loop with ceremony: "night-night, book. See you tomorrow." Books tucked in get chosen again.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "bookshelf" sits under a blue shelf with books lying on three shelves — a library the exact size of a toddler’s reach.

Ask your child

"Where do the books live?" "Can you pick a book?" "Where does the book go when the story is finished?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "book!" while reaching, march the book back to the shelf, or pat it goodnight — each one is the ritual taking root.

Out in the real world

Shelves are everywhere once named: the shop shelf, the library cart, grandma’s bookcase. "Books live on shelves" generalizes the tidy habit to every room in its life.

Try it together

Shelf Surprise: hide one small toy among the books and ask the shelf-keeper to find it — "check the bookshelf!" The shelf becomes a place worth visiting, and visitors keep it tidy.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do books live?" "Pick a book." (a reach) "Finished — where does it go?" Home. Point. Done.

This lesson pairs with the Bookshelf flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Bottle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "bottle" at real feeds first, then hands the tool over to a doll — because a toddler who feeds a teddy is rehearsing being fed, and rehearsed routines go smoother.

What is this?

A bottle is the small milk container with the yellow lid that many toddlers drink from — often the very first food word a family uses a dozen times a day.

What does it mean?

Bottle is a comfort word wrapped around a routine: naming it at every feed builds the mealtime vocabulary the cup, the plate and the spoon will inherit.

What does the child need to know?

You need the actual bottle (or the doll’s empty one) and the same two-beat script each time: name it before, name it after. "Bottle time… all gone!"

Why this matters

A named routine is a calmer routine: the word lands before the milk does, and a toddler who can predict the feed arrives at it peacefully.

What it teaches

Mealtime vocabulary, holding and tipping (hand strength and control), cause and effect — tip, swallow, empty — and pretend-play seeding for the teddy stage.

Words to learn

bottlemilkdrinkholdyummyall gone

Say this to your child

“"Bottle! Here is your bottle of milk. Two hands… hold it tight. Drink, drink — yummy! …All gone! Well done. Now, can teddy have a drink too? Feed the teddy!"”

Step by step

  1. Before the feed, hold the bottle up: "bottle! Time to drink."
  2. Guide two small hands around it — the hold is half the lesson.
  3. During: "drink, drink… yummy milk." The same words, every feed.
  4. After: "all gone!" — and let the toddler hand you the empty bottle. Handing in is a real job.
  5. Later at play, offer the doll bottle: "teddy is hungry — feed teddy!" Watch the whole routine replay in small hands.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "bottle" sits under a baby bottle with a yellow lid and the milk line showing — filled exactly to where a small drink stops.

Ask your child

"What is this?" "Where is the bottle?" "Can you feed teddy his bottle?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "baba," tap the bottle when thirsty, or tip the doll bottle to the teddy’s mouth with a sound effect — feeding vocabulary in action.

Out in the real world

Bottles appear at feeds, in bags, at grandma’s. Name them all — the word collects them. When the bottle finally retires, the card stays as the record of a first word well loved.

Try it together

Teddy Café: three "customers" (teddy, bunny, dolly) wait for their bottles. The barista feeds each one, on request, with the grown-up naming the order: "bottle for teddy!" Service with babble.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (bottle) "Where is the bottle?" (a point) "Feed teddy!" (a tip) — name, point, tip: the mealtime word is served.

This lesson pairs with the Bottle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Building Blocks — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "building blocks" through a shared tower — your block, their block, counted aloud — and ends in a crash that is permission, not mischief.

What is this?

Building blocks are the chunky colored blocks that stack into towers — the toddler engineering kit, complete with its own demolition phase.

What does it mean?

The block tower is early physics (balance), early maths (counting) and early manners (taking turns) built in one pile. The crash is the laboratory’s favourite experiment: what goes up comes down.

What does the child need to know?

You need floor space, a shared tower and the turn rhythm: "my block… your block." Count each landing. Announce the crash BEFORE it happens so the demolition is a plan, not a crime.

Why this matters

Blocks teach fail-safe persistence: a tower that falls is not a failure, it is the next game. That attitude is the whole foundation of learning anything harder later.

What it teaches

Grasp and release, hand-eye aim, balance intuition, counting-with-one-to-one-touch, turn-taking and cause-and-effect joy.

Words to learn

building blocksstacktowerupcrashagain

Say this to your child

“"Building blocks! Let’s build a tower. My block — one. Your block — two! My block — three… up, up, up… TALL tower! And now… crash it down! Again, again!"”

Step by step

  1. Spread the blocks: "building blocks!" — name while the hands find them.
  2. Place the first block: "my block. One."
  3. Offer the second: "your block… two!" Guide wobbles gently; wobble is data.
  4. Count every landing up the tower — the numbers climb with the blocks.
  5. The announcement: "tall tower… ready… CRASH!" Knock it down together, cheer, and start again — the rebuild is where the counting happens twice as happily.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "building blocks" sit under a tower of red, yellow, green and blue blocks — stacked the way every first tower stands: biggest bottom, proudest top.

Ask your child

"How many blocks in our tower?" "Whose turn now?" "What happens if we push it?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "more!", plant a block crooked and proud, or deliver the crash themselves with a drumroll — all of it is engineering.

Out in the real world

Towers live beyond the playroom: stone stacks in the garden, cups in the kitchen, sugar packets at the café. "Stack — like building blocks!" keeps the word earning.

Try it together

Knock-Down Countdown: build six high together, then count down 3-2-1 — the toddler delivers the crash on ZERO. Countdowns and crashes: the two best motivators ever invented for turn-taking.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are these?" (building blocks) "Stack them up!" (two or more placed) "What comes after tall?" (CRASH) — build, count, demolish: lesson complete.

This lesson pairs with the Building Blocks flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Changing Table — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "changing table" as the address of a routine — and gives the toddler one real job per change, which is how changes stop being wrestles.

What is this?

The changing table is the raised station where diaper changes happen — a place with a name, which is exactly what makes the routine predictable.

What does it mean?

Toddlers resist surprises more than diaper changes. A named place plus a named sequence (up, lie down, fresh diaper, all clean) converts a wrestle into a script everyone knows.

What does the child need to know?

You need the same short script every change and ONE job to hand over: carrying the diaper, peeling a tab, holding the cream. The job is not decoration — it is the cooperation.

Why this matters

A routine with an address and a script survives travel, grandparents and growth spurts. The words stay the same even when the world does not.

What it teaches

Routine vocabulary, body awareness (lie down, legs up), handing and fetching, and the first link in the chain that ends at the potty.

Words to learn

changing tablelie downdiaperfreshall cleandone

Say this to your child

“"Changing table! Up we go. Lie down, little one — there you are. Hold the diaper for me… thank you, helper! Fresh diaper… tabs… ALL CLEAN! Down you hop."”

Step by step

  1. Name the destination as you lift: "changing table! Up we go."
  2. Lay down with the same words: "lie down… there you are."
  3. Hand over the job: "hold the diaper — carry it for me!" The carrier is a helper, not a captive.
  4. Narrate the middle briefly: "fresh diaper… tabs… click."
  5. Finish with the fanfare: "ALL CLEAN!" and lift down — the same words, every single time, until the toddler pre-says them.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "changing table" sit under a blue changing table with yellow shelves — the station itself, ready and waiting.

Ask your child

"Where do diaper changes happen?" "Can you carry the diaper?" "What do we say at the end?" (all clean!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "table!" on the way, carry the diaper with ceremony, or announce "all clean!" before you do — the script is theirs now.

Out in the real world

Change stations live in cafés, malls and airports — named, they are familiar ports, not ambushes. The script travels with you.

Try it together

Dolly’s Change: the teddy or dolly gets the full routine at the "little table" — the toddler runs every step and every word. The expert teaching the expert.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do we change your diaper?" "Show me lie down." "What do we say at the end?" Address, pose, fanfare — the routine is owned.

This lesson pairs with the Changing Table flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Comb — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "comb" through a shared turn: the grown-up combs three strokes, then hands the comb over — because control shared is a battle halved.

What is this?

A comb is the toothed tool that tidies hair — it appears twice daily, which makes it one of the highest-frequency care words in the room.

What does it mean?

Hair care is body-ownership territory. A toddler who is handed the comb learns that their head is theirs AND that routines can be shared — the exact formula for every care routine to come.

What does the child need to know?

You need the comb, a willing head and the swap rule: three strokes each, counted out. The toddler’s strokes can land on teddy, on you, or on their own hair — any head counts.

Why this matters

The daily wrestle over hair is rarely about hair. It is about control. Sharing the tool converts the comb from something done TO the child into something done BY the family.

What it teaches

Tool grip, gentle-hand control, body-part vocabulary (hair, head), turn-taking and the ticklish business of self-grooming.

Words to learn

combhairgentlemy turnyour turntidy

Say this to your child

“"Comb! Time to comb your hair. My turn — one… two… three. Gentle, gentle. Now YOUR turn — comb teddy! Comb my hair! One… two… three. All tidy — look at that!"”

Step by step

  1. Present the comb: "comb! Time for tidy hair."
  2. Comb three slow strokes on the toddler: "my turn — one… two… three."
  3. Offer the swap: "your turn!" Hand it over handle-first.
  4. Accept any target: their hair, teddy’s fur, your head. Stroke count matters more than stroke target.
  5. Close with the mirror: "all tidy! Look at that hair." The finish line turns a chore into a reveal.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "comb" sits under a blue comb, teeth pointing the way it travels through hair.

Ask your child

"What is this?" "Whose turn is it?" "Comb teddy’s hair — gently!"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "my turn!", comb your hair with intense concentration, or pat the result in the mirror — control and pride arriving together.

Out in the real world

Combs appear at the barber, in grandma’s bag, at the pool. Every sighting is a rep: "comb! The hair-tidier." The word and the routine keep each other sharp.

Try it together

Salon Time: teddy, bunny and dolly queue up for the toddler’s salon. Three strokes each, gentle hands, "next customer please!" — the daily comb becomes a business.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (comb) "Show me gentle." (a soft stroke) "Whose turn after mine?" — name, touch, swap: tidy is taught.

This lesson pairs with the Comb flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Crayons — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "crayons" through a shared scribble — one crayon each, marks on paper, and the golden question: "tell me about your drawing."

What is this?

Crayons are the wax sticks that make colored marks on paper — the first drawing tools, and at this age the marks are scribbles with narratives attached.

What does it mean?

Scribbling is pre-writing and the narration is pre-literacy: a child who explains a scribble is learning that marks carry meaning, which is the whole secret of reading waiting downstream.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper taped down (the tape IS the trick — no sliding, no floor art), one crayon per hand and the question rule: "tell me about it," never "what is it?"

Why this matters

Being asked to narrate makes the child the author. Being asked to identify makes them the test-taker. Same scribble, opposite lessons — choose author.

What it teaches

Tripod grip seeds, mark control (pressure, direction), color words, narrative language and the sitting-focus that pencil work will later borrow.

Words to learn

crayonscolorsscribbledrawpapertell me

Say this to your child

“"Crayons! Let’s draw. Pick a crayon… I have green. Scribble, scribble! Look at the colors. Now — tell me about your drawing. Oh! It’s a car going to grandma’s? Tell me more!"”

Step by step

  1. Tape the paper, open the box: "crayons! Look at the colors — red, yellow, green, blue."
  2. Each choose one: "I pick green. You pick…?" — choice first, name second.
  3. Scribble side by side in silence for a minute. Companionable noise from the crayons only.
  4. Ask the golden question about THEIR page: "tell me about your drawing!" Listen. Follow the story wherever it goes — cars, monsters, grandma.
  5. Date and display: pin it up, or fridge-front it. An audience keeps authors writing.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "crayons" sits under five crayons standing in a yellow-and-green box — the toolkit, packed and ready.

Ask your child

"Which color is that?" "Tell me about your drawing!" "Can you make a big circle? A fast line?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might name colors while scribbling, narrate the story ("it’s a dog… running!"), or hand you a crayon and demand you draw — all of it is authorship.

Out in the real world

Color and mark live everywhere: the menu at the restaurant, chalk on the pavement, the shopping list. "I need my crayons for THAT!" is the sound of the word working.

Try it together

Story Gallery: three drawings, pinned in a row. A tour guide (the artist) walks you past each one and tells its story. Tickets are optional; pride is not.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are these?" (crayons) "Which color?" "Tell me about your picture!" — name, choose, narrate: the writer’s first lesson is done.

This lesson pairs with the Crayons flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Crib — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "crib" through a rehearsal: teddy goes to bed first, the same sentence lands at the rail every night, and the bed word becomes the period at the end of the day.

What is this?

The crib is the toddler’s own bed — bars, mattress, the yellow blanket — and the word that ends every day when it is said in the same place at the same time.

What does it mean?

"Crib" is a place word with a promise inside: sleep is next. Toddlers who can name the destination fight the journey less.

What does the child need to know?

You need the crib, one sentence and a teddy with a bed of his own (a shoebox works). The sentence — "into the crib, night-night" — is said at the rail, every night, until the child says it first.

Why this matters

Rituals are how toddlers tell time. The crib sentence is the last line of the day’s script; a known last line is what lets a small body let go.

What it teaches

Routine vocabulary, day-night sequencing, gentle transfer (the teddy tuck), and the self-settling that a predictable bed invites.

Words to learn

cribbedsleepnight-nightcozyteddy

Say this to your child

“"Crib! This is your crib — your very own bed. Cozy crib, soft blanket. Into the crib we go… night-night. Sleep tight. The crib is where sleep lives."”

Step by step

  1. At play, introduce teddy’s bed: "teddy is sleepy — into his crib! Night-night, teddy."
  2. Let the toddler do the tucking — sloppiness is love.
  3. Keep teddy’s routine shorter than theirs: he sleeps NOW so the idea is fresh tonight.
  4. At the real bedtime, the same sentence at the rail: "into the crib, night-night." Same words, same spot.
  5. Night after night, drop your voice a little more each word — the sentence itself becomes the wind-down.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "crib" sits under a blue crib with yellow bedding — the bed itself, made and waiting.

Ask your child

"Where do you sleep?" "Where does teddy sleep?" "What do we say at the crib?" (night-night!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "nigh-nigh" at the rail, tuck teddy unprompted, or climb in clutching the blanket — the word and the routine shaking hands.

Out in the real world

Beds are everywhere in books and lives — the baby’s crib, grandpa’s big bed, the dog’s basket. "Where does everyone sleep?" is a whole-car-ride game.

Try it together

Sleepy Zoo: every animal needs tucking into a "crib" (boxes, cushions, pots). The zookeeper tucks each one with the bedtime word. Lights out, zoo closed.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (crib) "Where do YOU sleep?" "Say it at the rail… what do we say?" Bed, point, night-night — the day can end now.

This lesson pairs with the Crib flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Diaper — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "diaper" by narrating the change in the same short words every time — and by giving the toddler one job, because busy hands do not protest.

What is this?

A diaper is the padded garment that gets changed many times a day — the most-repeated routine word in the toddler vocabulary by a mile.

What does it mean?

The diaper word is the first link in a chain: diaper → potty → toilet. Naming it kindly now makes every later link sound friendlier.

What does the child need to know?

You need the change script (lie down… fresh diaper… all clean!) and one job per change: fetch the diaper, carry it to the bin, hold the cream, choose front or back. One is plenty.

Why this matters

Changes happen a dozen times a day; that is a dozen vocabulary lessons and a dozen cooperation chances hiding in a routine everyone already does.

What it teaches

Body vocabulary, following a two-step instruction, carrying and bin-aiming (real hand-eye work), and potty-learning language seeded early.

Words to learn

diaperfreshcleanlie downbinall done

Say this to your child

“"Diaper! Time for a fresh one. Fetch the diaper… thank you! Lie down… fresh diaper… tabs click… ALL DONE! Now take it to the bin — in it goes! All clean."”

Step by step

  1. Before the change: "diaper! Time for a fresh diaper."
  2. Send the helper: "fetch the diaper, please!" — the fetch IS the lesson.
  3. Narrate in threes: "lie down… fresh diaper… tabs click."
  4. Assign the send-off: the toddler carries the old diaper to the bin — aim, drop, lid down.
  5. Close every time with "ALL DONE, all clean!" — the fanfare makes the routine applaudable.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "diaper" sits under a white taped diaper — the everyday object itself, plain as the routine it names.

Ask your child

"What do you need?" (a fresh diaper!) "Can you fetch the diaper?" "Where does the old one go?" (in the bin)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "diaper!" when wet, fetch it proudly, or slam the bin lid like a drum — the routine with sound effects.

Out in the real world

Diapers live in every bag and every shop. Spotting the pack at the store — "diapers! Our diapers!" — turns errands into vocabulary trips.

Try it together

Dolly’s Day: the doll needs FIVE changes. The parent-in-training runs each one — fetch, change, bin, fanfare. Repetition is the lesson; the doll never complains.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (diaper) "Fetch the diaper!" (a fetch) "Where does the old one go?" (bin) — name, fetch, aim: routine mastered.

This lesson pairs with the Diaper flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Easel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "easel" as the standing art station: paper clipped, arms up, big circles — the whole shoulder doing the work that writing will inherit.

What is this?

An easel is the standing frame that holds paper upright for drawing — here, the blue A-frame with the clip, at exactly standing height.

What does it mean?

Vertical surfaces change the drawing: the shoulder leads, the wrist follows, and the big-muscle work now is the small-muscle precision later. The easel is pre-writing dressed as art.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper, the clip (or a fridge, or a big box wall) and the one rule: marks live on the paper. Everything else — color, subject, enthusiasm — belongs to the artist.

Why this matters

High-energy toddlers focus better on their feet. The easel lets the body wiggle legally while the hands and eyes work — focus and movement, finally on the same side.

What it teaches

Shoulder and arm strength, vertical wrist position (the writing position), up-down and circle strokes, and the boundary discipline of one surface.

Words to learn

easelclippaperdrawcirclesup high

Say this to your child

“"Easel! Stand up tall — time to draw. Clip the paper… click! Big circles — round and round! Up, down, side to side… your arms are the engine. Look what you drew!"”

Step by step

  1. Clip the paper together: "easel! Paper goes on — click."
  2. Stand side by side, crayons up: "big circles first!" Draw giant loops shoulder-high.
  3. Vary the direction: "up… down… round and round." Name the strokes as they happen.
  4. Trade surfaces: their half, your half — mirror each other’s marks.
  5. The gallery finish: step back three steps, admire loudly, "shall we keep it or make another?" The artist decides.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "easel" sits under a blue art easel holding a white sheet — the standing studio, ready for its first masterpiece.

Ask your child

"What is this?" (easel) "Draw a big circle!" "Where does the paper go?" (on the easel, clipped)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "I draw!", fill the page with loops, or clip the next sheet themselves — the studio is now self-serve.

Out in the real world

Standing art hides in plain sight: fridge galleries, chalk walls, the whiteboard at the clinic. Any vertical surface is an easel with good PR.

Try it together

Wall Mural: tape a big paper sheet to the wall, artists take turns, one rule (paper only). The mural grows all week — a standing monument to the easel word.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (easel) "Where does the paper go?" (clipped on) "Show me a big circle!" — name, clip, circle: vertical art, unlocked.

This lesson pairs with the Easel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Floor Cushion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "floor cushion" as ownership and wind-down: this spot is YOURS, and the flop onto it — with the big sigh — is the game that practises calming down.

What is this?

A floor cushion is the round blue pad that lives on the floor — a toddler-sized seat that belongs to whoever flops on it.

What does it mean?

A defined personal spot does quiet work: it answers "where do I fit?", gives big feelings a retreat with dignity, and gives grown-ups a non-sentence way to say "take a beat."

What does the child need to know?

You need the cushion parked somewhere consistent (book corner is ideal) and the flop ritual: stand, wobble, FLOP, sigh. The sigh is not decoration — it is slow breathing, taught by comedy.

Why this matters

Calming down is a skill, not a temperament. Practised daily on a cushion, the flop-sigh becomes a tool the child can carry to any floor in the world.

What it teaches

Body regulation (the sigh), ownership vocabulary, sitting stamina for books, and the spatial word pair "on" and "off."

Words to learn

floor cushionmy spotsitflopsighcozy

Say this to your child

“"Floor cushion! Your very own soft spot. Watch me — wobble, wobble… FLOP! Aaaaah. Now you… FLOP! Big sigh! Cozy. This is where we read books and take soft landings."”

Step by step

  1. Introduce the spot: "floor cushion! This is YOUR spot."
  2. Demonstrate the flop: stand, wobble like a sleepy robot, FLOP — "aaaaah." Exaggerate the sigh; comedy is the teacher.
  3. Offer the turn: the toddler’s flop. Applaud the sigh especially.
  4. Park a book there: "your spot for stories." Read ON the cushion — the spot earns its job.
  5. On a stormy-feeling day, walk there together: "cushion time." No lecture, just the spot — the tool already knows what to do.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "floor cushion" sit under a round blue cushion — thick, soft and exactly the shape of a small sitting person’s landing.

Ask your child

"Where is YOUR spot?" "Show me the flop!" "Where do we read books?" (on the cushion)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "my cushion!", flop dramatically on request, or drag a book there unprompted — ownership announced.

Out in the real world

Personal spots scale up: the reading corner at the library, the window seat at grandma’s, the car seat that is "mine." Spots of one’s own are a lifelong need, started on foam.

Try it together

Cushion Island: cushions on the floor are islands, the floor is water — hop, flop, read, repeat. The game ends the way islands should: everyone flopped, everyone sighing.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (floor cushion) "Whose spot is it?" (mine!) "Show me the flop!" — name, own, flop: the soft spot is claimed.

This lesson pairs with the Floor Cushion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

High Chair — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "high chair" as a word said on the walk to the kitchen — the same word, the same moment, every meal, so the sitting-down starts before the food does.

What is this?

The high chair is the tall toddler seat with the tray — where every meal happens, and where most mealtime battles are quietly won or lost before any food arrives.

What does it mean?

The climb-in is the meal’s first course. A named seat, a known climb and one tray job give the meal a calm opening — which the food then keeps.

What does the child need to know?

You need the word at the right moment (on the walk to the kitchen, never from across the house), a hand for the climb and one tray job before plates land: spoon placed, cup parked, bang delivered.

Why this matters

Mealtime meltdowns are usually opening-scene meltdowns. A named, ritualised climb-in removes the surprise — and a toddler who chose to climb resists less than one who was placed.

What it teaches

Routine vocabulary, climbing control, tray-side object permanence (cup goes HERE), and the meal-start patience that eating cooperatively needs.

Words to learn

high chairclimbuptraysityummy

Say this to your child

“"High chair! Time to eat. Climb up… up you go! The tray clicks on — ready! Park your cup… there. Bang the spoon — hello, spoon! Now… yummy time."”

Step by step

  1. On the walk to the kitchen, the word: "high chair time!" — same tone, same moment, daily.
  2. The climb: offer a hand but let the leg-work be theirs. "Up you go — you did it!"
  3. The tray job before the food: "park your cup… click the spoon… ready!" A prepared tray is a prepared toddler.
  4. Eat beside them and name the good moments: "sitting tall — yum yum."
  5. The close: "all done!" — hands washed, cup to the sink. Meals that end on purpose start on purpose tomorrow.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "high chair" sit under a blue high chair with a yellow tray — the seat itself, tray open for business.

Ask your child

"Where do you sit for meals?" "Can you climb up?" "Where does your cup go?" (on the tray)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "chair!" at the kitchen door, climb up half-alone, or park the cup exactly on the spot — the routine, self-run.

Out in the real world

Eating seats are everywhere: the café high chair, the booster at grandma’s, the picnic bench. "Time for your eating chair!" keeps the rule traveling.

Try it together

Restaurant Night: the high chair is Table One, the teddies have Table Two. Menus (pictures), orders taken, trays prepared by the head waiter. Meals begin better when they are staged.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do meals happen?" (high chair) "Show me climb up!" "Where does the cup park?" — word, climb, park: seated and smiling.

This lesson pairs with the High Chair flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Laundry Basket — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "laundry basket" through the in-and-out game toddlers are already obsessed with — and hides a real chore inside it, one garment at a time.

What is this?

A laundry basket is the woven container that holds the clothes — and, in this room, occasionally one giggling toddler.

What does it mean?

Containers are toddler physics 101: in, out, full, empty. The basket card meets the obsession head-on and borrows its momentum for tidying.

What does the child need to know?

You need the basket, a small pile of laundry on the floor and the one-piece rule: fetch ONE thing, drop it in, say what it was — "socks IN!" Repetition is the engine; the peekaboo is the dessert.

Why this matters

Chores at two are not chores — they are games with a finish line. The one-piece fetch is the smallest honest version of laundry day, and it counts.

What it teaches

In-out spatial concepts, carrying and dropping (aim!), item naming, following a repeated instruction, and the earliest work pride there is.

Words to learn

laundry basketinoutfetchsocksfull

Say this to your child

“"Laundry basket! The clothes go IN. Fetch one thing… the socks! Socks IN. Now the shirt… shirt IN. Towel IN! Look — the basket is FULL. And where is YOU? In the basket! Peekaboo!"”

Step by step

  1. Present the basket: "laundry basket! The clothes live here."
  2. Model one fetch: "socks — IN!" Drop with ceremony.
  3. Hand over the job: "your turn — fetch ONE thing!" One at a time; the count is the game.
  4. Name every landing: "shirt in! Towel in!" The basket fills; the vocabulary does too.
  5. The finale: "is anything ELSE left?" — and the toddler, if willing, climbs in. "IN the basket! Peekaboo!" Empty basket, full victory.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "laundry basket" sit under a blue woven basket — handles up, ready to hold the whole week’s wash.

Ask your child

"Where do the clothes go?" "Fetch ONE thing!" "Is the basket full or empty?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "IN!" on every drop, fetch items nobody asked for (enthusiasm!), or climb in before being asked — the schema demands it.

Out in the real world

Baskets live in every room: toy baskets, market baskets, the basket at the till. "That goes IN the basket!" scales the word to the whole house.

Try it together

Basket Post: the basket becomes a letterbox — toys "post" socks and clothes through the handles. Deliveries all afternoon; the laundry happens on schedule.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (laundry basket) "Put the socks IN!" "Full or empty?" — name, drop, fill: the container word is in.

This lesson pairs with the Laundry Basket flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Night Light — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "night light" by handing over the switch: the child turns the dark friendly themselves, which is the whole trick.

What is this?

A night light is the small glowing lamp that stays on through the night — the friendly face a dark room makes when a toddler is in it.

What does it mean?

Dark-room fears bloom around two. The night light works because it hands over agency: the child flicks the switch, the child names the light, the dark becomes managed — not banished, managed.

What does the child need to know?

You need the light at toddler-height reach and the ritual order: bath, pajamas, THEN the click. The click is the child’s job; the "night-night, night light" is the close.

Why this matters

A light the grown-ups sneak in later is a patch; a light the child switches on is a tool they run. Agency converts fear into competence — one click at a time.

What it teaches

Cause and effect (click, glow), routine sequencing, self-soothing with a named tool, and the confidence of operating something real.

Words to learn

night lightdarkglowclickonnight-night

Say this to your child

“"Night light! Time for your job. Click… ON! Look — the room is dark, but the night light glows. Soft and yellow. It watches over you all night. Night-night, night light!"”

Step by step

  1. At bedtime, present the switch: "night light! Your job — the click."
  2. Guide the finger, then fade the guide: click — "ON comes the night light!"
  3. Name what changed: "the room is dark BUT the night light glows. Yellow and soft."
  4. Say goodnight to it by name: "night-night, night light. Watch over me."
  5. Repeat the ritual identically nightly — sameness is what makes the click powerful.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "night light" sit under a glowing plug-in lamp, light spilling yellow around it — the dark room’s one friendly face.

Ask your child

"Who turns on the night light?" (you do!) "What color does it glow?" "What do we say to the night light?" (night-night!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "I click it!", announce "light ON!" at dusk, or wave goodnight to the glow — agency in action.

Out in the real world

Lights that guard live everywhere: the hallway night light at grandma’s, the hotel bathroom glow, the porch light. "A night light!" — the tool travels.

Try it together

Glow Hunt: dim the room in daytime play and find all the soft glows — night light, clock, phone (from afar). The dark gets mapped; mapped things stop being scary.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who clicks the night light?" (me!) "What does it do?" (glows) "Say goodnight to it…" — click, glow, goodnight: the dark is staffed.

This lesson pairs with the Night Light flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Pajamas — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "pajamas" through the dressing script — arm in, leg in, ZIP — and crowns the zip as the toddler’s official job, tonight and forever.

What is this?

Pajamas are the one-piece sleep suit with the yellow zip — the official uniform of bedtime, and the second hand on the bedtime clock.

What does it mean?

The pajama word is a signal: clothes, then teeth, then story, then crib. Same order nightly is what makes each step believable to a small body.

What does the child need to know?

You need the suit laid out and the three-part script said in the same order every night. The zip is non-negotiable child territory — guide the start, let the finish be theirs.

Why this matters

A child who does the zip ends the dressing as the owner of it. Ownership at the zip leaks upward into ownership of the whole bedtime.

What it teaches

Dressing vocabulary (arm, leg, zip), two-hand coordination, sequencing, and the pride loop that makes tomorrow night easier.

Words to learn

pajamassleepy clothesarm inleg inzipcozy

Say this to your child

“"Pajamas! The sleepy clothes. Arm in… leg in… now YOUR job — the zip! Hold it… pull… ZIIIP! All zipped — cozy pajamas! Bedtime team is dressed."”

Step by step

  1. Lay the suit flat: "pajamas! The sleepy clothes."
  2. Script the arms: "arm in… other arm in!" — the child pushes limbs through where they can.
  3. Script the legs: "leg in… leg in… wiggles check!"
  4. Hand over the zip: "your job — the zip! Hold the bottom… up you go… ZIIIP!" (Guide the tab into the carter, then let them pull.)
  5. Admire: "cozy pajamas — bedtime team, dressed!" Straight into the next routine step so the sequence locks in.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "pajamas" sits under a blue one-piece suit with the yellow zip down the front — the uniform, standing to attention.

Ask your child

"What are these?" (pajamas!) "Where does the arm go?" "Whose job is the zip?" (mine!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "zip!" with both hands ready, demand pajamas at the first yawn, or zip a jacket at breakfast for practice — the job is loved.

Out in the real world

Zips are everywhere: jackets, bags, tents. "Just like your pajama zip!" makes every zipper a practice rep for the big one.

Try it together

Dress the Teddy: teddy’s "pajamas" (a sock with a hole, ceremonially) go on arm-in-leg-in while the toddler narrates. The zip is the finisher — teddy’s or a bag’s, any zip counts.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are these?" (pajamas) "Show me arm in!" "Whose job is the zip?" — name, dress, zip: the bedtime team reports ready.

This lesson pairs with the Pajamas flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Picture Book — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "picture book" as a pointing game: the child’s finger finds, the grown-up names, the book gets read again — and again — and the tenth read is the best one.

What is this?

A picture book is a book whose pictures carry the story — here, the one with the teddy on the cover — and at this age reading IS the pointing game played on its pages.

What does it mean?

Point-and-name builds vocabulary faster than any screen because the picture holds the meaning while the adult holds the voice. Repetition is not laziness — it is the curriculum.

What does the child need to know?

You need the book, a lap and the finger rule: the CHILD’S finger does the finding. The adult’s job is naming whatever the finger lands on — no agenda, no skipping ahead.

Why this matters

The tenth read of the same book is when the child starts "reading" it from memory — turning pages, naming the bear, finishing the lines. That is real reading, months before letters.

What it teaches

Vocabulary by pointing, book handling (page turning is a skill), attention stamina, and the book-love that everything later stands on.

Words to learn

picture bookbookpointpagereadagain

Say this to your child

“"Picture book! Let’s read. Open it up… point to something! Your finger says… a dog! Woof. Now a ball! Point again… What do you find? Read it again? Of course!"”

Step by step

  1. Cover first: "picture book! Look — a bear on the cover. Hello, bear!"
  2. Open together; the child’s finger leads: "where do you point?"
  3. Name what the finger finds: "a dog! A ball! A tree!" — no steering, just naming.
  4. Turn pages by the corner — let the page-turn be their skill, clumsy and cherished.
  5. The close: "finished… AGAIN?" Repeat at will. The tenth read is the goal, not the failure.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "picture book" sit under a book with a teddy bear on the cover under a sunny sky — a story waiting on the shelf’s friendliest face.

Ask your child

"Where is the bear?" "Point to the dog!" "Turn the page…" "Read it again?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might name a picture from memory, "read" aloud in babble-story, or bring the book as a request — reading, arriving early.

Out in the real world

Books live in every room and every bag. A book at breakfast, a book at the clinic: "picture book time!" The habit outruns the venue.

Try it together

Book Picnic: three books, one cushion, snacks for the grown-up. The child "reads" each to the audience — page turning, pointing, babbling narration. The critic’s favourite: the one read forty times.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (picture book) "Point to the bear!" "Turn the page!" — cover, point, turn: reading has begun.

This lesson pairs with the Picture Book flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Pillow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "pillow" through the flop: wobble like a sleepy robot, land on the pillow, sigh like the day is over — because it is.

What is this?

The pillow is the soft square at the head of the bed where the tired head lands — the last stop of every bedtime.

What does it mean?

The flop-sigh is secret training: the exaggerated sigh slows the breathing, and slow breathing is the body’s own sleep switch. Comedy first, physiology second.

What does the child need to know?

You need the pillow (on the bed, not the floor), a teddy for rehearsal and the three-beat game: wobble… flop… "aaaaah." The sigh is the star; coach it proudly.

Why this matters

Toddlers cannot be ordered to relax, but they can be invited to perform a sigh. The game rehearses the exact exhale that falling asleep needs — nightly, joyfully, free.

What it teaches

Body regulation, head-neck control in the flop, routine vocabulary, and the muscle memory of exhale-and-settle.

Words to learn

pillowheadflopsighsoftmmm

Say this to your child

“"Pillow! The soft, squishy pillow. Wobble like a sleepy robot… flop! Your head lands… aaaaah. Mmm. The pillow holds your head all night. Goodnight, head!"”

Step by step

  1. Daytime rehearsal: teddy flops first — "wobble, wobble… FLOP! aaaaah." The toddler attends to the comedy.
  2. Offer the turn: the toddler’s flop onto the pillow. Coach the sigh: "bigger… aaaaah!"
  3. Name the landing: "your head on the pillow — mmm, soft."
  4. At bedtime, the same three beats, slower: wobble (a sleepy sway), flop (head down), sigh (long and soft).
  5. Fade the comedy, keep the sigh: within a week the flop IS the goodnight.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "pillow" sits under a plump blue pillow — the square, soft landing every bedtime promises.

Ask your child

"Where does your head go?" (on the pillow) "Show me the flop!" "What does the sigh sound like?" (aaaaah)

What your child can say or do

Your child might flop and sigh on request, demand "flop again!", or land mid-yawn at bedtime — the tool, self-deploying.

Out in the real world

Pillows are universal: the sofa cushion, grandma’s guest pillow, the pool lounger. Any soft landing is "a pillow moment" — sigh included.

Try it together

Pillow Mountain: every cushion in the house, one summit, flops all round. The expedition ends flat, sighing, gloriously done.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (pillow) "Where does the head land?" "Show me the sigh!" — name, flop, exhale: sleep is approaching.

This lesson pairs with the Pillow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Play Mat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "play mat" as playtime’s frame: unrolling is the starting whistle, toys live on the mat, and the roll-up is the finish line everyone can see.

What is this?

The play mat is the rolled blue pad that unrolls into the floor’s play surface — the stage every toy performs on.

What does it mean?

A defined play space solves sprawl: toys stay in the kingdom, tidy-up has a border, and the words "on" and "off" get a home with edges.

What does the child need to know?

You need the mat and the two rituals: the unroll ("tadaaa! play time!") and the roll-up ("toys home… roll, roll… all done!"). Both belong to the child as soon as hands allow.

Why this matters

Beginnings and endings are what toddlers need most. A mat that visibly starts and stops play gives the day’s chaos a shape — and shape is calm.

What it teaches

Spatial words (on, off, edge), rolling motor skills, sequencing (open, play, close), and boundary respect that transfers to every surface in life.

Words to learn

play matrollunrollon the mattidydone

Say this to your child

“"Play mat! Roll it out — tadaaa! Play time! The toys go ON the mat… on the mat… on the mat. And when play is done: toys home, roll it up… all done! The mat sleeps."”

Step by step

  1. The opening ceremony: the child unrolls — "tadaaa! The play mat! Play time!"
  2. Set the kingdom’s law gently: "toys live ON the mat." Scatter a few on purpose and ask: on or off?
  3. Play. The mat does its silent work while everyone forgets it is there.
  4. The finish: "toys go home on the mat… roll, roll, roll — ALL DONE!" The roll-up is the ending the day needs.
  5. Park the rolled mat in its spot: "the mat sleeps here. See you next play!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "play mat" sit under a rolled blue mat with a fold of it unrolled — mid-birth, on its way to being the floor’s playground.

Ask your child

"Where do the toys live?" (on the mat) "Is the ball ON the mat or OFF?" "What do we do at the end?" (roll it up!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "on the mat!" while tidying, unroll it solo with a tadaaa, or roll toys INTO the mat for fun — the border, understood.

Out in the real world

Mats scale up: picnic blankets, beach towels, gym mats. "Our play mat!" generalizes the kingdom to the park, the pool, the lawn.

Try it together

Mat Islands: cushions and mats across the floor are islands in the "sea" (the bare floor). Cross only by mat-hops. The border IS the game.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (play mat) "Where do toys go?" (on the mat) "Show me roll it up!" — unroll, play, roll: playtime framed.

This lesson pairs with the Play Mat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Potty — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "potty" early and casually — the word meets the child long before the training does, so the little chair is an old friend by the time it matters.

What is this?

The potty is the toddler’s own little toilet — the blue chair with the yellow seat — and the word that the whole transition will be built on.

What does it mean?

Potty learning is a language project before it is a skill project: children need the words (potty, pee, poo, flush) long before the timing clicks. Fear shrinks when naming comes first.

What does the child need to know?

You need the potty visible and casual — in the bathroom, never a surprise — and the teddy demonstration. NO pressure, NO performance: the card’s job this week is just the word.

Why this matters

Families who name the potty early report smoother training: the tool is familiar, the words are shared, and the child walks in curious instead of ambushed.

What it teaches

Body-awareness vocabulary, imitation (the teddy sits), routine sequencing (pants down, sit, wipe, flush), and the patience that training will test.

Words to learn

pottysitpeepooflushbig kid

Say this to your child

“"Potty! This is the potty — your little chair. Teddy is sitting… well done, teddy! Want to try? Pants up is fine — just sitting. One day, pee and poo go in the potty. Big kid stuff!"”

Step by step

  1. Show and name, zero drama: "potty! This is YOUR potty — your very own little chair."
  2. The teddy demo: teddy "sits" on the potty. "Teddy is trying! Well done, teddy."
  3. Invite a clothed sit: the toddler tries it, pants up, for the novelty. "You sit on the potty!"
  4. Seed the words at every change: "one day, pee and poo will go IN the potty — big kid stuff!"
  5. Leave the door open, literally: the potty stays visible, unremarkable, ready. The word keeps working between lessons.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "potty" sits under a blue potty chair with a yellow seat — small, sturdy and exactly child-sized.

Ask your child

"What is this?" (potty!) "Where does teddy sit?" "Who has a potty?" (you do!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce "my potty!", sit the teddy repeatedly, or request a clothed sit at odd hours — curiosity, correctly aimed.

Out in the real world

Toilets are everywhere in a child’s world: at home, at grandma’s, the little cubby at the café. Each one is "a potty for big people" — the family of the word.

Try it together

Potty School: every doll and bear sits on the potty in turn while the toddler-teachers narrate: "sit… wait… well done!" The classroom runs itself.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (potty) "Whose potty is it?" (mine) "Where does teddy sit?" — name, own, demo: the word is in place before the training is.

This lesson pairs with the Potty flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Puzzle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "puzzle" through the handover: one piece at a time, the trying narrated out loud, and the CLICK celebrated as what it is — persistence paying off.

What is this?

The puzzle is the four-piece wooden board — four bright pieces, four matching holes, and the toddler’s first lab of matching and patience.

What does it mean?

Puzzles teach the fail-again muscle: a piece that will not go in is not broken, it is turned wrong. The grown-up’s calm voice while trying is the actual curriculum.

What does the child need to know?

You need the board, the pieces in YOUR hand (one at a time) and the narration: "turn it… flip it… try again… it FITS!" Never grab the piece; the struggle is the school.

Why this matters

Four pieces is victory-sized: enough challenge to demand trying, not enough to flood. Finishing builds the identity — "I am someone who finishes" — worth more than the skill itself.

What it teaches

Shape matching, wrist rotation, visual scanning, frustration tolerance, and the one-to-one logic of piece-into-hole.

Words to learn

puzzlepieceturntry againfitsclick

Say this to your child

“"Puzzle! Four pieces, four spots. Here is one — try it… turn it… click! It fits! This one is tricky… turn… flip… try again… CLICK! All four — finished! Puzzle champions!"”

Step by step

  1. Empty the board together: "puzzle! Four pieces, four spots."
  2. Hand over ONE piece: "try it… turn it around… CLICK! It fits! Red in red."
  3. The next piece resists: narrate the calm: "hmm… turn it… FLIP it… try again… CLICK!"
  4. Fade your words as the trying improves — the child inherits the narration.
  5. The finish: lift the whole board and pour the pieces out — "AGAIN!" The second round runs smoother than the first; that is learning, visible.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "puzzle" sits under a four-piece wooden board in red, yellow, green and blue — every piece out, every hole waiting.

Ask your child

"Where does the red piece go?" "Turn it… now what?" "What do we say when it does not fit?" (try again!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "click!" on every fit, narrate their own trying, or pour the pieces out unprompted — persistence with a sound effect.

Out in the real world

Fitting lives everywhere: keys in doors, toasters, shape sorters, the last piece of toast in the bag. "It fits — like your puzzle!" keeps the skill hunting.

Try it together

Mystery Piece: hide one piece under a cup while the child closes their eyes — which piece is missing? Find it, place it, repeat. Deduction joins the matching.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (puzzle) "Show me try again!" "What happens when it clicks?" (it fits!) — try, flip, click: persistence installed.

This lesson pairs with the Puzzle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Shoes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "shoes" at the door, where the word works: foot in, foot in, and the Velcro rip that is the toddler’s signature on getting dressed.

What is this?

Shoes are the blue-and-yellow sneakers that mean OUTSIDE — the most exciting dressing word in the language, because it always predicts adventure.

What does it mean?

The shoe word works because its reward never varies: shoes on, we go out. A word with a perfect track record gets believed — and said — early.

What does the child need to know?

You need the shoes, a sitting spot by the door and the ceremony: present each shoe, foot in, then hand over the Velcro. The rip is the child’s job; never do it for them.

Why this matters

Dressing battles shrink when the child owns the finisher. The Velcro rip is tiny, loud and theirs — the exact size of job that makes a two-year-old invincible.

What it teaches

Foot-eye coordination (the aim into the shoe), grip strength for the rip, left-right body awareness, and dressing-sequence pride.

Words to learn

shoesfootVelcroriponoutside

Say this to your child

“"Shoes! Where are your shoes? There they are! One foot — in! Other foot — push! Now YOUR job… rip the Velcro! RIIIIP! Shoes on… let’s go OUTSIDE!"”

Step by step

  1. By the door, the word: "shoes! Shoes on means we go OUT!"
  2. The ceremony: present the first shoe like a crown — "one foot… IN!"
  3. Second shoe, their push: "other foot… push… THERE!"
  4. Hand over the rip: "your job — rip the Velcro! RIIIIP!" Both shoes, both rips, both celebrations.
  5. Straight out the door: the word’s reward arrives on schedule, every time, which is why it never needs teaching twice.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "shoes" sits under a pair of blue and yellow sneakers — laced, waiting, facing the door.

Ask your child

"Where are your shoes?" "Which foot goes in first?" "Whose job is the Velcro?" (mine!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "shoes!" at the door, race to sit on the step, or rip the Velcro with a war cry — adventure, formally opened.

Out in the real world

Shoes live in racks, by doors, under beds — and on everyone else. "Look, daddy’s shoes! Baby’s shoes!" is a matching game the whole family plays.

Try it together

Shoe Shop: every shoe in the house on display, the toddler is the shopkeeper — "trying on" each pair (one foot only is fine), ripping every strap in stock. Fittings daily.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are these?" (shoes) "Where do feet go?" (in the shoes) "Whose job is the rip?" — name, aim, rip: out the door.

This lesson pairs with the Shoes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Sippy Cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "sippy cup" with the two-hand lift — the child’s first owned drink — and the park-it finish that gives the cup (and the meal) an ending.

What is this?

The sippy cup is the blue cup with the green lid and two handles — the bridge between bottle and open cup, and the first drink the child runs alone.

What does it mean?

Drinking is a full skill stack: grip, lift, tip, swallow, park. Naming the cup claims it — MY cup — and ownership is what makes practice self-driven.

What does the child need to know?

You need the cup at every meal and the script: "two hands… lift… sip sip sip… put it down." The park is real: the cup has a spot, and parking it ends the sip.

Why this matters

Two hands before one: the two-hand grip is the training wheels of drinking. Mastered here, the open cup arrives months earlier — and the floor stays drier.

What it teaches

Two-hand grip and lift, tip control (the difference between a sip and a shower), swallowing coordination, and object-parking (a place for everything).

Words to learn

sippy cuptwo handsliftsipput downmy cup

Say this to your child

“"Sippy cup! Here is YOUR cup. Two hands… lift… sip sip sip. Tiny tips! …All done? Put it down — park it in its spot. Good drinking, my friend!"”

Step by step

  1. Present at mealtime: "sippy cup! YOUR cup."
  2. Script the lift: "two hands… one, two… LIFT… sip sip sip."
  3. Coach the tip small: "tiny tips — just a little! …perfect."
  4. The park: "all done sipping? Put it DOWN — in its spot." Point to the spot; parking becomes automatic.
  5. Fade the script word by word over weeks until "cup!" triggers the whole routine solo.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "sippy cup" sit under a blue cup with a green lid and two handles — gripped exactly the way two small hands will grip it.

Ask your child

"Where is your cup?" "How many hands?" (two!) "Where does the cup go after?" (in its spot)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "my cup!", lift with exaggerated two-handed care, or park it unprompted — independence, one sip at a time.

Out in the real world

Cups are everywhere: the café’s lid cup, grandma’s special cup, the big people’s mugs. "Someday, a cup like that — first, master THIS one." The ladder is visible.

Try it together

Cup Picnic: every teddy has a cup, the toddler serves each one — "teddy’s cup… bunny’s cup!" — then drinks their own with the two-hand script. Hosting and hydration, together.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (sippy cup) "How many hands lift it?" (two) "Where does it park?" — grip, sip, park: the drink is owned.

This lesson pairs with the Sippy Cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Soap — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "soap" inside the sink ceremony: water on, soap on, rub the fronts, rub the backs, rinse — the same five beats every wash, until the hands do it themselves.

What is this?

Soap is the pink bar (or the pump) that makes the bubbles that take the germs away — the hero of the first hygiene habit a child ever owns.

What does it mean?

Hand-washing is the most reusable routine in the whole set: it travels from this sink to every sink for life. The ceremony structure — same order, sung — is what makes it stick.

What does the child need to know?

You need the sink, the soap at reach and the five-beat script, sung or chanted: "wet… SOAP… rub the fronts… rub the backs… RINSE!" The child’s jobs: pressing the pump, the rubbing, the rinsing.

Why this matters

Germs are invisible, but bubbles are not. The bubbles give the child proof of work — "look, soap is ON!" — which is why the soap step can never be skipped.

What it teaches

Sequencing (five steps in order), rubbing strength and coverage, water-temperature respect (grown-up checks), and the lifetime habit itself.

Words to learn

soapbubbleswashrubrinseall clean

Say this to your child

“"Soap! Time to wash. Water on — wet hands. SOAP — press! Bubbles! Rub the fronts… rub the backs… between the fingers… RINSE! The bubbles take the germs away. ALL CLEAN — sparkly hands!"”

Step by step

  1. Walk to the sink naming the destination: "soap time! Hands get washed here."
  2. Beat one, water: "wet the hands… woosh."
  3. Beat two, the star: "SOAP! Press the pump… look — bubbles!" (Or rub the pink bar.)
  4. Beats three and four: "rub the fronts… rub the backs… between the fingers!" Twenty seconds, sung.
  5. Beat five, the close: "RINSE! Watch the bubbles go… ALL CLEAN!" Towel, fanfare, exit — the ceremony owns the germs.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "soap" sits under a pink bar of soap — smooth, plain and exactly as bossy as a good hygiene hero should be.

Ask your child

"What makes the bubbles?" (soap!) "Where do we wash?" (at the sink) "What do we say at the end?" (all clean!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "soap!" at every sink sighted, pump twice (enthusiasm), or sing the rub song solo — the ceremony, self-run.

Out in the real world

Sinks follow children everywhere: restaurants, clinics, airports. The ceremony travels with them — five beats, any basin, germs lose.

Try it together

Doll Wash Day: the dolls’ hands need washing too! The toddler runs the full five beats for each customer. Standards are high; bubbles are mandatory.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes bubbles?" (soap) "Show me rub the fronts!" "What comes after rinse?" (all clean!) — press, rub, rinse: the habit is built.

This lesson pairs with the Soap flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Socks — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "socks" as the gateway dressing skill: stretchy, forgiving, and the first garment a toddler can genuinely put on alone — with cheers.

What is this?

Socks are the pair of blue foot-covers that come before shoes — stretchy, matchable and perfectly designed for small hands to learn on.

What does it mean?

The sock teaches two ideas at once: the dressing pull (over toes, up the heel) and the pair concept — two the same, one per foot. Matching and dressing in one tiny garment.

What does the child need to know?

You need the pair and the start position: YOU begin the sock over the toes, the child does the pulling-up. The heel-hitch can wait; the pull is tonight’s win.

Why this matters

Self-dressing starts where resistance is lowest. A sock pulled up by its owner is a two-minute win that funds the courage for shirts, pants and zips later.

What it teaches

Pinch-grip and pull, over-the-toes coordination, pair matching (find the twin!), and the left-right body mapping that dressing quietly builds.

Words to learn

sockstoespulluppaircozy toes

Say this to your child

“"Socks! One sock… over the toes… pull, pull… UP! Now the other sock — find the twin! There it is! Over the toes… pull… UP. Two socks — cozy toes! You did your feet yourself!"”

Step by step

  1. Present the pair: "socks! Two the same — a pair!"
  2. Start one sock over the toes: "over the toes… now YOU — pull, pull, UP!"
  3. The heel is optional: "almost… there! Cozy toes!" Progress over precision.
  4. The hunt: "where is the other sock? Find the twin!" Matching under the bed is half the lesson.
  5. Repeat on the second foot — then the mirror check: "TWO socks — you dressed your feet!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "socks" sits under a pair of blue socks — heel to toe, folded the way pairs wait in the drawer.

Ask your child

"Where are the socks?" "Find the other sock!" "Who pulled it up?" (me!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "socks on!", hunt the twin with detective energy, or pull socks onto hands as mittens (innovation) — dressing, claimed.

Out in the real world

Sock pairs run the whole house: laundry lines, drawer sortings, the mysterious single sock. "Find its pair!" is a chore-seed and a matching drill in one.

Try it together

Sock Match-Up: six socks, three pairs, mixed on the floor. Match them all, then dress the teddy in the loosest pair. Sorting, pairing, grooming — one basket of socks.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are these?" (socks) "Where do they go?" (on the feet) "Show me pull UP!" — over toes, pull, twin: feet dressed by their owner.

This lesson pairs with the Socks flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Stacking Rings — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "stacking rings" by letting the toy do the teaching: the big ring will not sit on the small ring, and the discovery is the lesson.

What is this?

The stacking rings are the rainbow stacker on its yellow post — five rings from biggest to smallest, and the size rule hiding inside every try.

What does it mean?

Ordering by size is first maths. The stacker teaches it the best way possible — physically: wrong order simply does not work, so the hands discover what words would take weeks to explain.

What does the child need to know?

You need the stacker and the discipline NOT to correct: hand the rings in random order, let the tries happen, narrate only the wins. The post is the patient teacher.

Why this matters

Children remember what they discover. A ring that refuses to stack teaches "big at the bottom" more durably than any instruction — and the joy is undamaged because nobody failed.

What it teaches

Size comparison (big, bigger, small), trial-and-error problem-solving, posting accuracy (ring to peg), and color words riding along free.

Words to learn

stacking ringsbigsmallbiggestfirstrainbow

Say this to your child

“"Stacking rings! Ring on the post… ooh, that one will not go! Try the BIG one first — whoosh, down it goes! Now the next… and the next… teeny tiny on top! A rainbow tower!"”

Step by step

  1. Empty the post: "stacking rings! Where do they go — ON the post!"
  2. Hand rings in mixed sizes. Say nothing about order; watch the experiments.
  3. Narrate the discovery when it happens: "the BIG ring — whoosh, down to the bottom!"
  4. Name the wins as the tower grows: "red… green… yellow… and the teeny tiny one — TOP!"
  5. The remix: unstack and line the rings up on the floor, biggest to smallest — a rainbow snake. Same lesson, new shape.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "stacking rings" sit under the rainbow stacker on its yellow post — every ring off, the tower waiting to happen.

Ask your child

"Which ring is the biggest?" "Where does the big ring go?" (bottom!) "Which one goes on top?" (the tiny one)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce "big one FIRST!", swap a wrong ring without drama, or roll the rings across the floor (physics is also on the syllabus) — ordering, discovered.

Out in the real world

Size ordering is everywhere: nesting cups, the Russian dolls at grandma’s, plates in the cupboard. "Big to small — like your rings!" finds the maths hiding in kitchens.

Try it together

Ring Race: two players, two posts, same pile — who builds the rainbow first? (Nobody loses; both towers are celebrated, then knocked down with ceremony.)

Understanding check

Ask: "Which is the biggest?" "Show me the tiny one!" "Where does big go?" (first — the bottom!) — size, order, tower: maths in colors.

This lesson pairs with the Stacking Rings flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Stroller — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "stroller" as the family vehicle: the climb is the child’s job, the buckle’s click is the finisher, and teddy’s stroller rehearses the whole ride.

What is this?

The stroller is the blue pushchair by the door — the vehicle that carries little legs when little legs are done, and the routine word that makes leaving the park survivable.

What does it mean?

The stroller word lives where friction lives: getting in, getting out, leaving the fun. A named climb-in-click script turns the two worst moments of any outing into known steps.

What does the child need to know?

You need the stroller, the climb (child-powered with a hand nearby) and the click: the final buckle snap belongs to the child. Then the teddy stroller for rehearsal at home.

Why this matters

A child who climbs in themselves and clicks themselves is a passenger with ownership — and passengers with ownership disembark with dignity when the ride is over.

What it teaches

Climbing control, buckle manipulation (fine motor), leaving-the-fun transitions, and the pushing-the-teddy empathy loop.

Words to learn

strollerclimb inbuckleclickpushoff we go

Say this to your child

“"Stroller! Climb in — up you go! Buckle the straps… and CLICK! You did it. Off we go — wheels go round! And when the ride is done, click again — you hop out, big and safe."”

Step by step

  1. At the stroller: "stroller! Time to climb in."
  2. The child-powered climb — hand hovering, not hauling: "up you go!"
  3. Buckle together, child finishes: "click! Ready to roll."
  4. At home, the rehearsal: teddy rides the toy stroller — "push teddy… teddy is safe and cozy!" The driver learns what passengers feel.
  5. On outings, the same two words every time: "stroller — climb in!" and "stroller — click!" Sameness is the secret.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "stroller" sits under a blue pushchair — seat back, wheels ready, parked exactly where the outing begins.

Ask your child
