"Where do you ride?" (the stroller) "Who clicks the buckle?" (me!) "Where does teddy sit?" (in HIS stroller)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "stroller!" at the park gate, climb and click unprompted, or push teddy on serious rounds — the vehicle, fully staffed.

Out in the real world

Strollers park outside shops, fold into cars, queue at airports. Every sighting is a name-check: "stroller — like yours!" The word rides along.

Try it together

Teddy Bus Route: the toy stroller does the circuit — teddy on at the sofa stop, off at the kitchen stop, next passenger please. The toddler is driver, conductor and mechanic.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (stroller) "Who clicks the buckle?" "Show me climb in!" — climb, click, ride: the family vehicle is run by its passenger.

This lesson pairs with the Stroller flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Stuffed Bunny — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "stuffed bunny" through the find-the-part game: ears, nose, paws, tail — found on the bunny first, then on the child, which is how body words travel.

What is this?

The stuffed bunny is the cream plush rabbit with the long ears — the soft friend who will spend the next decade listening to everything.

What does it mean?

A loved toy is the safest classroom: every part of the bunny can be named, touched and giggled over, then found again on the child’s own body. The transfer is nearly automatic.

What does the child need to know?

You need the bunny and the two-step find: "where are bunny’s EARS?" (point) "Where are YOUR ears?" (point). Four parts is a full lesson: ears, nose, paws, tail.

Why this matters

Body vocabulary lands best on something the child adores — and lands twice as well when it hops onto their own body in the same breath.

What it teaches

Body-part vocabulary, pointing accuracy, gentle-touch practice, and the pretend-play seed: bunny will soon eat, sleep and get "poorly" on schedule.

Words to learn

stuffed bunnyearsnosepawstailhop

Say this to your child

“"Stuffed bunny! Soft bunny, long ears. Where are bunny’s ears? …There! Where are YOUR ears? …There! Bunny’s nose… YOUR nose! Bunny’s paws… YOUR hands! Now — hop hop hop, little bunnies!"”

Step by step

  1. Hello the friend: "stuffed bunny! Soft bunny — say hello!"
  2. Find on the bunny: "where are bunny’s EARS? …There! Long, soft ears."
  3. Transfer: "and where are YOUR ears? …There! You have ears too!"
  4. Repeat for nose, paws (hands!), tail — bunny first, child second, every time.
  5. The finale: "bunny hops! Can YOU hop?" Two hops and a hug close the lesson — and open a decade of friendship.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "stuffed bunny" sit under a cream plush rabbit — ears up, paws forward, the gentlest teacher in the room.

Ask your child

"Where are bunny’s ears?" "Where are YOUR ears?" "How does a bunny move?" (hop!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "bunny!" with a hug, point to their own nose proudly, or hop-hop across the room — vocabulary, hopping.

Out in the real world

Plush friends travel: in the car, to the clinic, to bed. Each carries the game — "bunny’s nose… your nose!" — to every waiting room in town.

Try it together

Bunny School: the child teaches the bunny ITS body parts — "this is your nose, bunny!" Teaching reverses the game and doubles the vocabulary. Every pupil needs a name; the child supplies it.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where are bunny’s ears?" (point) "Where are YOUR ears?" (point) "Hop like bunny!" — find, transfer, hop: body words, delivered by a friend.

This lesson pairs with the Stuffed Bunny flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Table and Chair — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "table and chair" as the toddler’s workstation: activities happen here, and the push-in of the chair is the signature at the bottom of every finished job.

What is this?

The table and chair are the child-sized yellow table and its green-and-red seat — furniture built to toddler scale so little legs sit flat and little arms reach everything.

What does it mean?

A defined workspace does what it does in any office: it tells the body "this is where work happens," and the push-in tells it the work is finished. Montessori’s oldest trick, still undefeated.

What does the child need to know?

You need the table set for ONE activity at a time and the closing ritual: pieces in the box, crayons in the tub, chair pushed in. The push-in is always the child’s.

Why this matters

One activity out, one activity away gives the morning a rhythm the child can predict — and predictability is where focus comes from.

What it teaches

Sitting stamina, workspace respect, task completion (open-do-close), and the body mechanics of a proper seated reach.

Words to learn

tablechairsitworkpush inall done

Say this to your child

“"Table and chair! This is your work spot. Sit on the chair… scoot in… the puzzle lives here today. We work… we finish… pieces in the box — and push your chair in! All done. What a worker!"”

Step by step

  1. Invite to the seat: "table and chair! Sit on YOUR chair… scoot in."
  2. One activity, ready on the tabletop: "today the puzzle lives on the table."
  3. Work together, narrating lightly — the table is where focus lives.
  4. The finish line: "all done! Pieces in the box… crayons in the tub…"
  5. The signature: "push your chair in… CLICK-scoot. Job complete!" Admire the pushed-in chair like a signed painting.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "table and chair" sit under a small yellow table with a green and red chair — child-height, ready for one activity and no more.

Ask your child

"Where do we work?" (at the table) "Whose chair is this?" (mine!) "What do we do when we finish?" (push it in!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might scoot in unasked, refuse all other chairs ("MY table!"), or push the chair in with a flourish — the workstation, staffed.

Out in the real world

Work tables scale: the kitchen table for baking, the desk at school one day, the picnic bench. "Your table!" generalizes the habit to every surface ahead.

Try it together

Café Table One: the table hosts a rotating menu — puzzle at ten, crayons at eleven, snack at noon. The maître d’ (the toddler) seats every guest and pushes in every chair.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do we work?" (table) "What do we push when we finish?" (the chair) "Show me scoot in!" — sit, make, push: work has an address.

This lesson pairs with the Table and Chair flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Teddy Bear — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "teddy bear" as the class pet: the teddy eats first, brushes first, sits first and sleeps first — rehearsing every routine in this set before the toddler’s turn.

What is this?

The teddy bear is the brown plush bear with the round tummy — the classic first friend, dragged by one arm through every meal, nap and adventure.

What does it mean?

The teddy is both comfort and curriculum: whatever the child does to the bear, the child is rehearsing. A teddy who eats, brushes and sleeps on schedule makes those routines normal, expected, done.

What does the child need to know?

You need the bear and the rehearsal plan: today teddy joins one routine FIRST — feeding, or teeth, or bed. The child plays parent; you narrate. Never force the teddy on the child; invite.

Why this matters

Big feelings talk to bears more easily than to grown-ups, and new routines rehearse better on bears than on tired toddlers. The bear is the safest practice ground in the house.

What it teaches

Empathy and care-taking (the parenting instinct, born), routine sequencing, gentle-hand control, and the comfort-object bond that travels to bed and back.

Words to learn

teddy bearhugfeedgentlesleepynight-night

Say this to your child

“"Teddy bear! A soft brown bear. Hug him — gentle squeeze! Teddy is hungry… feed him… yummy, teddy! Now teddy’s teeth — brush brush. And NOW teddy is sleepy… into the crib! Night-night, teddy. You take such good care of him."”

Step by step

  1. Hello the bear: "teddy bear! Give him a gentle hug — squeeze!"
  2. Pick ONE routine for rehearsal: "teddy is hungry! Feed teddy his spoon."
  3. The child feeds; you narrate: "one bite for teddy… yummy! Now a drink."
  4. Extend gently: teddy’s teeth get brushed, teddy sits on the potty, teddy gets his blanket — one per sitting, never all at once.
  5. Close with the goodnight: "teddy is sleepy — night-night, teddy." The whole routine chain, run by the smallest parent in the house.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "teddy bear" sit under a brown plush bear with a round tummy — arms open for the hug that starts every lesson.

Ask your child

"Where is teddy?" "Can teddy have a hug?" "What does teddy need now — food? Brush? Bed?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might feed teddy bite by bite, demand his toothbrush, or tuck him with a kiss — the smallest parent on the block, fully qualified.

Out in the real world

Bears ride in baskets, sit at cafés, visit clinics. Every outing with the bear is a rehearsal tour — "teddy is watching the doctor too!" Comfort travels; routines follow.

Try it together

Teddy’s Full Day: a picture schedule for the bear — eat, play, wash, bed — and the child runs the whole day on schedule. A day parenting a teddy is a week of cooperation in the real routine.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where is teddy?" "Give him a gentle hug!" "What does teddy do first at night?" (brush teeth / pajamas — any step named wins) — hug, care, rehearse: the friend is on the team.

This lesson pairs with the Teddy Bear flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Toothbrush — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "toothbrush" through the handover: the child brushes first (munching allowed), the grown-up finishes, and the same four-line song counts the whole thing down.

What is this?

The toothbrush is the blue brush with the yellow stripe — a twice-a-day-for-life tool, which makes the toddler years the perfect installation window.

What does it mean?

Brushing fails as a fight and works as a ritual: the child goes first (control), the grown-up finishes (quality), the song is the timer (no clocks, no battles).

What does the child need to know?

You need the brush, a rice-grain of fluoride paste, the you-then-me order and the four-line song: "round and round, round and round, front and back, all done!" Spitting finishes the show.

Why this matters

The handover order solves both problems at once — the child’s need for control and the parent’s need for clean teeth. And the song outlasts the resistance.

What it teaches

Oral-motor control, sequencing, the habit loop itself, and the tolerance for someone else’s hands in their mouth that dental visits will need.

Words to learn

toothbrushteethbrushround and roundspitall clean

Say this to your child

“"Toothbrush! Time to brush the teeth. Your turn first — round and round, round and round, front and back… my turn — the back ones, quick quick… spit! ALL CLEAN. Sparkly smile!"”

Step by step

  1. Present at the sink: "toothbrush! Time for teeth."
  2. Rice-grain of paste on the brush — "tiny toothpaste, plenty!"
  3. Child brushes first: "your turn — round and round!" Munching the bristles is normal; keep going.
  4. The handover: "my turn — let me get the back ones." Quick, gentle, non-negotiable, done in twenty seconds.
  5. The song ends, spit, admire: "ALL CLEAN — sparkly smile!" Same order, both sessions, every day.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "toothbrush" sits under a blue and yellow brush — bristles up, ready for the twice-daily ceremony.

Ask your child

"Where is your toothbrush?" "Whose turn is first?" (mine!) "What do we do at the end?" (spit! all clean!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sing the brush song while eating, demand "MY turn first!", or brush the teddy’s teeth with his own brush — the habit, spreading.

Out in the real world

Brushes live in cups, travel kits and hotel bags. A new setting is the ritual’s test — same song, same order, any bathroom on Earth.

Try it together

Brush the Family: teddy’s teeth, dolly’s teeth, then the child’s — the whole roster, in order, one song each. The clinic visit rehearses itself here.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (toothbrush) "Who brushes first?" (me) "What does the song say?" (round and round!) — paste, brush, handover: installed for life.

This lesson pairs with the Toothbrush flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Towel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "towel" as the bath’s grand finale: wrapped like a burrito, dried in the same named order every time — head, tummy, toes — and the body words come free.

What is this?

The towel is the big blue wrap that ends every bath — and the named drying order is one of the friendliest body-parts lessons ever disguised as a routine.

What does it mean?

Drying in a fixed order does two jobs: the bath gets a predictable, cozy ending, and head-tummy-toes becomes a body map the child can recite on their own skin.

What does the child need to know?

You need the towel and the order: "towel dries the HEAD… towel dries the TUMMY… towel dries the TOES!" Same order every bath. The child’s job: drying a doll the same way.

Why this matters

The end of the bath is where escapes happen — the naked sprint down the hallway. A named, ceremonial drying routine catches the child inside the towel and the routine.

What it teaches

Body vocabulary, wrap tolerance (sensory), following a three-step order, and the care-task rehearsal that doll-drying provides.

Words to learn

toweldrywrapheadtummytoes

Say this to your child

“"Towel! Time to get dry — wrap you up like a burrito! Snug and warm. Towel dries the HEAD… towel dries the TUMMY… towel dries the TOES! All dry! Now you dry the dolly — head, tummy, toes!"”

Step by step

  1. Arms open at the bath’s end: "towel time! Into the big dry hug."
  2. Wrap like a burrito, snuggle tight — the wrap IS the game.
  3. Dry in the named order, slow and warm: "towel dries the HEAD… the TUMMY… the TOES!"
  4. Hand over a second towel and a doll: "your turn — dry the dolly. Head… tummy… toes!"
  5. The exit: "all dry, all cozy — bath finished!" The same order next bath, and the body words stick for good.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "towel" sits under a folded blue towel — thick, soft and waiting at the end of every bath.

Ask your child

"Where does the towel dry first?" (the head!) "Where does it dry last?" (the toes) "Can you dry the dolly?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce the order unprompted ("head! tummy! toes!"), wrap themselves, or dry every doll in the house — the ceremony, self-run.

Out in the real world

Towels follow swims, spills and rainy days. Beach towels, hand towels, the towel at grandma’s — the word and the order travel to every bath and every pool.

Try it together

Towel Shop: every doll and bear gets a full wash-and-dry service — bath (a bowl), wrap, the named drying order, tipped well. The launderette never closes.

Understanding check

Ask: "What dries you after the bath?" (the towel) "What dries first?" (head) "Show me the wrap!" — wrap, order, dry: cozy and complete.

This lesson pairs with the Towel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Toy Car — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "toy car" through the ramp-and-garage circuit — and hides the stop-and-go words inside the game, where they will drive every ride after this one.

What is this?

The toy car is the little red car with the blue wheels — usually the first vehicle a toddler pushes, and the first story with wheels on it.

What does it mean?

Push-and-go teaches cause and effect; stop-and-go teaches the words that make play a language. The car is small enough to master and fast enough to love.

What does the child need to know?

You need the car, a cushion ramp and a shoebox garage. The script: "vroom vroom… STOP at the light… GO!" The words do the teaching; the car does the motivating.

Why this matters

Traffic words (stop, go, fast, slow) are the most-reusable transport vocabulary in the set — they show up at every crossing, every bath cup, every spoon. Learned on a toy car, they are already home.

What it teaches

Pushing aim and force control, ramp physics (up the cushion, down the floor), stop-go inhibition (the freeze is a real skill), and first pretend narration.

Words to learn

toy carvroompushstopgofastslow

Say this to your child

“"Toy car! Vroom vroom — push it! Up the cushion… and down — wheee! Stop at the light… now GO! Fast, fast… slow, slow… STOP! Park it in the garage — night-night, car. Again!"”

Step by step

  1. The floor first: "toy car! Push it… vroom vroom!" Chase it together.
  2. Build the cushion ramp: "up the hill… and DOWN — wheee!" Repeat until physics feels owned.
  3. The shoebox garage: "park the car — night-night, car." Parking ends a lap; the lap can begin again.
  4. The words: "stop at the light… GO! Fast… slow… STOP!" The freeze is part of the game — hands off the car at STOP.
  5. Two cars, two players: one for you, one for them — the first shared race, with all the traffic words doing the talking.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "toy car" sit under a little red car with blue wheels — the exact shape of the first vehicle to cross a living-room floor.

Ask your child

"Where is the car?" "Make it GO!" "Freeze — what do we say?" (STOP!) "Fast or slow?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "vroom!" while pushing, slam the car to a halt at STOP, or narrate the whole journey — the driver’s licence, early.

Out in the real world

Cars are everywhere: the street, the car park, the pushchair’s wheels. "Real cars go fast… SLOW at the crossing!" — the toy taught the street’s words.

Try it together

Car Wash: the shoebox becomes a carwash — the car drives in, gets "sponged" with a facecloth, drives out sparkling. Wash, park, vroom: the full municipal service.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (toy car) "Make it fast… now SLOW!" "Where does it sleep?" (the garage) — push, stop, park: driving is fluent.

This lesson pairs with the Toy Car flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Toy Drum — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "toy drum" through the copy-cat game: loud, soft, fast, slow — the whole first music curriculum, ending on STOP, hands up, giggle.

What is this?

The toy drum is the red drum with the yellow rims and two sticks — the loudest friend in the room and the first instrument a toddler can truly play.

What does it mean?

Drumming is listening practice disguised as noise: copying a rhythm demands attention. The loud-soft contrast also plants the inside-voice idea in a place where it is FUN.

What does the child need to know?

You need the drum, the sticks and the copy-cat rule: I play, you play. The four contrasts — loud/soft, fast/slow — then STOP, sticks up. The stop is part of the music.

Why this matters

A child who can play loud AND soft owns both volumes. That ownership is the foundation the inside voice gets built on — and the drum is where it is the most fun to practice.

What it teaches

Rhythm copying (attention!), wrist control, dynamic contrast (loud/soft), inhibition on the stop, and the listening half of all music.

Words to learn

toy drumbangloudsoftfastslowstop

Say this to your child

“"Toy drum! Bang bang BANG — loud! Now soft… soft, soft. Copy me — loud! …soft! Fast fast fast… slooow. And… STOP! Sticks up high! Your turn — I’ll copy YOU!"”

Step by step

  1. Introduce the sticks: "toy drum! Bang bang BANG — loud!"
  2. The contrast: "now softly… soft, soft taps." Model with a whisper-face.
  3. Copy-cat: you play loud, they play loud; soft, soft; fast; slow. Four rounds, four contrasts.
  4. The stop: "and… STOP! Sticks up!" Freeze with the sticks in the air — the funniest rule in music.
  5. The encore: their turn to lead, you copy. The teacher seat is the real prize.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "toy drum" sit under a red drum with yellow rims and two crossed sticks — the volume of the room, about to change.

Ask your child

"Bang LOUD!" "Now soft…" "What do we say at the end?" (STOP!) "Your turn — teach me!"

What your child can say or do

Your child might lead the copy-cat game, whisper-tap theatrically, or freeze mid-bang with sticks aloft — dynamics, mastered.

Out in the real world

Loud and soft live everywhere: the vacuum (loud), the cat (soft), the library (whispers). "Drum rules — soft inside!" transfers the whole lesson to daily life.

Try it together

The Volume Song: bang the four contrasts in a fixed order with the song, ending on STOP — the same order daily until the child plays it solo for an audience of teddies.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (toy drum) "Show me loud… now soft!" "Where do the sticks go at STOP?" (up high!) — bang, contrast, stop: the first concert, complete.

This lesson pairs with the Toy Drum flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.

TODDLER ROOM LESSON · TODDLER ROOM · AGES 1–3 YEARS

Toy Train — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches "toy train" as a journey: over the cushion mountain, through the chair tunnel, stop at the station — position words riding behind the little green engine.

What is this?

The toy train is the green engine with its red trim and two carriages — wheels that connect, a line that grows, and the chugga-chugga that carries position words for free.

What does it mean?

The train game is a preposition festival: over, under, through, round, stop. Every lap lands the words again — and the station stop teaches journeys have endings.

What does the child need to know?

You need the train and a course: cushion mountain (over), chair tunnel (under), rug lake (round). The station is a shoebox. The words name each obstacle as the train meets it.

Why this matters

Position words are the grammar of a toddler’s physical world — and the train repeats them with the enthusiasm only a chuffa-chuffa can supply.

What it teaches

Position/spatial words, tracking a moving object, sequencing (mountain, then tunnel, then station), and the pretend-narration that stories grow from.

Words to learn

toy trainchoo choooverunderstopstation

Say this to your child

“"Toy train! Choo choo! Chuffa chuffa… OVER the cushion mountain… UNDER the chair tunnel… round the rug lake… and STOP at the station! All aboard! Next stop — the sofa! Chuffa chuffa choo choo!"”

Step by step

  1. The first lap together: "toy train! Choo choo — chuffa chuffa chuffa!" Push it round the rug.
  2. The mountain: "OVER the cushion — up and over!" Name it as the wheels climb.
  3. The tunnel: "UNDER the chair — through the dark! …Out the other side!"
  4. The station: "STOP at the station — all aboard! Next stop: the sofa!" Passengers (small toys) board; the service expands.
  5. The child drives the route solo, narrating if they can — you ride as a passenger and ask: "what comes next?"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "toy train" sit under a green engine with red trim and two little carriages — coupled and ready, the journey about to start.

Ask your child

"Where does the train go?" (over! under! round!) "What does the train say?" (choo choo!) "Where does the journey end?" (the station)

What your child can say or do

Your child might say "choo choo!" through the tunnel, invent new stops ("grandma’s!"), or couple more carriages on — the network, expanding.

Out in the real world

Trains run through every town: the level crossing, the platform, the track under the bridge. Watching a real train after the toy is a revelation — "choo choo, but ENORMOUS!"

Try it together

Night Train: dim the lights, the engine’s headlamp (a torch) leads the route — over, under, through, station. Same words, new drama. Passengers: everyone, teddies included.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is this?" (toy train) "Where does it go?" (over, under, round) "Where does it stop?" (the station) — chuff, climb, stop: the journey is fluent.

This lesson pairs with the Toy Train flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Toddler Room.
